articles.title: Anthrax Unlocks Boss Level
articles.description: Forty-five years after their formation, Anthrax continues to be one of the most influential and beloved bands in heavy music. Coming together in New York City, the group released a pair of albums—1984’s Fistful of Metal and the following year’s Spreading the Disease—that, along with a ferocious live show (they supported Black Sabbath and Metallica early on), established the five-piece as one of the forefathers of thrash metal. Anthrax’s third album, 1987’s Among the Living, was the breakthrough that put them in the pantheon of thrash greats. The critically acclaimed record, which eventually went gold, helped the band graduate from clubs to arena stages and cemented their place in the Big Four of American thrash alongside Metallica, Megadeth, and Slayer. “It's been the fucking privilege of a lifetime to get to do this,” guitarist and co-founder Scott Ian tells PG. “We connected deep enough into the planet with Among the Living that essentially we’ve been able to have a career for 40 years since.” In the years that followed, Anthrax zagged when other bands zigged. But remaining true to their own musical ideals is what allowed them to stand out from the metal pack. After being name-checked by Public Enemy on 1987’s “Bring the Noise,” Anthrax eventually recorded a version of that song with the Long Islanders in 1991 and followed with a joint tour, one of the landmark early metal-rap crossover pairings. In 1992, the band appeared on the Fox sitcom Married… with Children, playing a show at the Bundy residence, which replicated a 1989 MTV stunt where they trashed a contest winner’s (if you want to call them that) own house. Those years alone would secure Anthrax’s legacy. But the band is nowhere near the nostalgia circuit. Now, a decade after For All Kings, their 11th and most recent studio album, Anthrax have finally followed it up, with the new Cursum Perficio. Bringing Cursum Perficio to life took nearly six years. Anthrax wrapped the three-year touring cycle for For All Kings in November 2019, a run that included shows celebrating the 30th anniversary of Among the Living. Over dinner after their final show, at Mohegan Sun in Connecticut, the band agreed to take some time off before starting on the follow-up. Drummer Charlie Benante had some rough demos, and the plan was for him, Ian, and bassist Frank Bello to get together in early 2020 and jam out instrumentals. First, Ian was going to finish a new album with Motor Sister, his side project with Joey Vera of Armored Saint, Jim Wilson of Mother Superior, John Tempesta (White Zombie, The Cult) and his wife, vocalist Pearl Aday. Instead, Covid hit, and like nearly everyone else in the world, he was stuck at home. For the next few years, the band worked remotely, zapping files and parts back and forth online. “Not since the band started touring in 1984 have I ever been literally in one place for that long, let alone my house with my wife and my son,” Ian says. “Nobody knew anything. Nobody knew if we were ever going to play again.” There was also plenty of anxiety about the unknown, the horrors of school shootings, partisan division, and cutthroat capitalism, as well as the tragedy of losing his father-in-law, the artist known as Meat Loaf, who passed away in 2022. All of it informed Ian’s lyrics. “If you want to put it in gamer speak, we beat some final boss and we got to the next level of who we are as songwriters." —Scott Ian” “So much of that is certainly where I was at the time when I was writing lyrics for the record and my energy making the record, and I would have to think the same as for Charlie,” Ian says. “About 90 percent of the music is from his demos, and Frankie came in with fully realized stuff as well, and is also amazing at writing melody ideas. But most of it starts with Charlie.” In early 2022, the trio finally got together at Dave Grohl’s Studio 606 in the San Fernando Valley. Immediately, they realized they were onto something bigger than just another late-career album. They’d begin with one of Benante’s riffs or rough arrangements, which would quickly turn into a skeleton of a song. “I remember that demo for ‘The Edge of Perfection,’” Ian says, “and I was thinking, ‘Holy fuck!’ If this is all we have, we're in good shape.’” He’s not wrong. The song, built on Benante’s original demo, Bello’s chorus melody and groove-heavy bass line, and Ian’s words, runs for nearly seven minutes, with an atmospheric instrumental opening that explodes in a blast of metal riffing, aided by Joey Belladonna’s towering vocals. Benante has compared the song to Anthrax classics like “Only” and “Indians,” and Ian agrees with that sentiment, saying it ranks among the top tunes in the Anthrax catalog. “I think it's the best song we've ever written,” he says. “That's my hot take on my own song that I'm a part of. When people ask, ‘What's your favorite Anthrax song?’ I usually say "Caught in a Mosh,’ based on the fact that it’s the one that's never been out of our set since that record [Among the Living] came out. But I just think on ‘Edge of Perfection’ we got to some other level, you know? Or, if you want to put it in gamer speak, we beat some final boss and we got to the next level of who we are as songwriters.” Once the trio had the songs where they wanted them, they sent them to lead guitarist Jon Donais. Stuck at his home in Massachusetts, away from his bandmates, Donais had used the downtime to practice, and he says it made him a better player. When it came time to cut his parts, he’d get the tracks back with timestamps marking where the others wanted him to play. He’d cut a demo, take notes from Benante and Ian, then record a final version. Because the songs were already so strong, he says, he had room to get creative. “Right off the bat, I knew it was going to be great and I had to have something great cooking,” Donias recalls. Far from cramping his creativity, the isolation felt familiar to Donais. He says the process was much the same on For All Kings, his first album with the band. Now 13 years in, making him the longest-tenured lead guitarist in Anthrax history, he was at ease with the setup, and he quickly heard how the new songs connected to the band’s classic material. “It has some old-school Anthrax vibes to it, and is a well-rounded record,” he says, then adds, “It’s got some curveballs too.” One he didn't see coming: the black metal influence on “The Edge of Perfection.” “It has some old-school Anthrax vibes to it, and is a well-rounded record. It’s got some curveballs, too." —Jon Donais” One early fan of that song was Dave Grohl. After mixing it at Grohl’s Studio 606, and with Grohl having played Ian the new Foo Fighters album before its release, Ian returned the favor. “I sent him ‘The Edge of Perfection’ and ‘It’s for the Kids,’ which is a love letter to Anthrax fans,” Ian says. “He wrote me back the next day—I'm paraphrasing—‘Dude, like, holy shit! Oh my God, ‘Kids’ is classic Anthrax.” And about ‘Edge,’ he said, ‘It’s so you guys, and so new at the same time.’” The reception has proved Grohl right. On social media, fans hailed the song as unmistakably Anthrax, and some called it one of the best releases from any of the Big Four in years. Benante’s pulsating drums, Ian and Donais’ guitars, and Belladonna’s vocals all contribute, but what seems to be connecting most is Ian’s lyric. The song, he says, is about choosing to live by love rather than fear, and sticking with that choice for the long haul. It also argues that perfection is boring and that real beauty is in facing life’s challenges, having empathy, and constantly working to keep yourself in a good place. Navigating the intricacies of that song gave Anthrax confidence, fueling a heavy and urgent sound that permeates the entire album. “Listening to it, I know where we were mentally when we were working on the demos,” Ian says. “How happy we were with the material we had… it’s all over the record. We've never had a moment like that, ever, in the history of the band. This is bigger than us. This one is special.” The album’s title, when translated from Latin, has several meanings: My journey has come to an end; My journey is over; I complete my journey. But have no fear—it’s not a sign that Anthrax is ready to call it quits. “We're not necessarily coy about it because we answer the question,” Ian says. “When people ask us, ‘Is it the last record?’ ‘Are you saying goodbye?’ I don't sit there and go, ‘Well, maybe…’ That’s not us.” In fact, the title came from an unexpected place. “Nobody knew anything. Nobody knew if we were ever going to play again.” —Scott Ian” “Charlie came up with the idea after he read that a stone at Marilyn Monroe’s [home] had it,” Ian says. “He found out what it meant, and he just really loved the meaning and the feeling of the phrase. So much of it has to do with the journey to make this record.” If you need more proof that the band isn’t done, the music makes the case. The 11-song album packs as powerful a punch as any Anthrax album in recent memory. In addition to previously released tracks, the tone-setting instrumental “Persistence of Memory” and the ferocious “Everybody’s Got a Plan” are sonically adventurous indicators of a group that isn’t ready to take a victory lap quite yet. The response so far has been incredibly strong. Anthrax played a small club gig at Brooklyn’s Saint Vitus ahead of a stadium show with Iron Maiden and Megadeth, and on the band’s European run this past summer, Donais says, “It's for the Kids” went over big with crowds. At a time when they could be winding down, Anthrax continue to play hard and loud. "Their journey to Cursum Perficio hasn't been easy, but as Ian considers where they've arrived after 45 years, he's very aware of the payoff." “Nobody hands you this,” Ian says of the band’s career. “I wasn't this person in another life. I wasn't this person in two other lives. Growing up in my life, it's been a road to get here.” Anthrax Gear Scott Ian Guitars Jackson X Series Signature Scott Ian King V (primary guitar, for rhythm parts; “white, the first one they built me”) Overdubs done with Gretsch Malcolm Young “Salute” Jet Jackson American Series soloist (pink) Gibson Les Paul Custom Amps Marshall JCM800 EVH 5150IIIS EL34 100W Effects KHDK Scott Ian Sgt D TC Electronic Booster + Distortion Gamechanger Audio Plasma Strymon Cloudburst MXR EVH Phase 90 Beetronics Zzombee Filtremulator “The KHDK and the TC Electronic were used in front of a Marshall JCM800 as part of my main rhythm tone.
